note: The second consumer of the Lexicon's shared underline (site/lexicon.css / site/lexicon.js): a small set of LOAD-BEARING figures per page, marked in the HTML as <span class="rcpt" data-rcpt="<id>">, each with a record here. site/receipts.js reads this file, builds the popover card for each marked figure, and adds the page's 'Show the receipts' toggle only if the current page has at least one entry. Deliberately NOT exhaustive -- see PART A2 of outputs/22_SIGNATURE_UX_AND_GAME_LADDER.md: marking every number would make the marked ones mean nothing. Every record needs either `tool` (a script in tools/ that produced or checked the figure) or `source` (a citation for a figure this site measured against or quotes from a primary source) -- checked by tools/check_receipts.py, which also confirms every data-rcpt id in the HTML has a record here and vice versa, and that every `tool` path actually exists on disk.

fields.id: stable slug, matches the HTML span's data-rcpt
fields.page: the page this figure lives on
fields.value: the figure as it reads on the page, exactly
fields.formula: the derivation, if the page states one -- omit rather than invent
fields.inputs: the inputs that formula was run with
fields.tool: path under tools/ that computed or checked this, if this site did the computing
fields.source: a citation, if the figure is an external measurement this site quotes or checked itself against
fields.verified_at: the date this was last checked
fields.falsifier: one sentence: what would make this figure wrong, or what it leaves out
fields.claim: optional -- a slug in data/claims/, if this figure bears on a live prediction

receipts.inputs: r = p/p_th = 1/10 · target p_L = 10⁻¹²
receipts.falsifier: excludes routing, magic-state factories and correlated noise, which all sit on top of this bare per-qubit count.

receipts.inputs: r = p/p_th = 1/3 · target p_L = 10⁻¹²
receipts.falsifier: the same bare-count caveat as qec-1057: routing and magic-state overhead are not included.

receipts.formula: fit of log(logical error rate) against distance across a d = 3, 5, 7 series
receipts.inputs: Google Willow processor, per-two-distance-step suppression
receipts.source: Google Quantum AI, Nature 638, 920 (2025); arXiv:2408.13687
receipts.falsifier: the single d = 5 → 7 step alone reads closer to 2.1 — the 2.14 figure is the whole-series fit, not any one step.

receipts.value: under half a million physical qubits
receipts.formula: state-of-the-art Shor circuit re-costing, surface-code assumptions
receipts.inputs: <1,200 logical qubits · <90M Toffoli gates · physical error rate ≈ 10⁻³
receipts.source: Gidney, Babbush, Drake, Boneh et al. (Google Quantum AI / Ethereum Foundation / Stanford), arXiv:2603.28846 (Mar 2026)
receipts.falsifier: a 2022 estimate under the same assumptions put this at 1.9 billion — the algorithmic side (not hardware) closed most of that three-order-of-magnitude gap, and could move again.

receipts.formula: precomputable half of Shor's algorithm depends only on public curve parameters
receipts.inputs: runs from the moment a transaction reveals its public key, inside the confirmation window
receipts.source: Gidney, Babbush, Drake, Boneh et al., arXiv:2603.28846 (Mar 2026)
receipts.falsifier: applies to exposed-key coins specifically — it is an upper bound on how fast the racing attack could run, not a claim about coins whose keys have never been revealed.

receipts.formula: surface-code cost to break one key inside a 10-minute confirmation window
receipts.inputs: physical error rate ≈ 10⁻³, 2022 circuit constructions
receipts.source: Webber et al., AVS Quantum Science 4, 013801 (2022)
receipts.falsifier: superseded by arXiv:2603.28846's 2026 re-costing (btc-500k) — this figure is kept on the page as the before-picture of a four-year, three-order-of-magnitude collapse, not as today's estimate.

receipts.formula: the byte length of a real ML-DSA-65 signature, generated and measured live in the visitor's own browser
receipts.inputs: WebCrypto-backed ML-DSA-65 sign operation, this page's own instrument
receipts.source: FIPS 204 (ML-DSA); several secondary sources instead quote round-3 Dilithium3's 3,293, which this page's own measurement corrects
receipts.falsifier: measures the FIPS-204-final scheme specifically — an implementation still on the round-3 Dilithium spec would legitimately measure 3,293.

receipts.formula: the byte length of a real SLH-DSA-128s signature, generated and measured live
receipts.inputs: WebCrypto-backed SLH-DSA-128s sign operation
receipts.source: FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA)
receipts.falsifier: the 's' (small) SLH-DSA parameter set trades signature size for slower signing — the 'f' (fast) set has a different, smaller signature at a speed cost this page does not measure.

receipts.formula: 10 segments × 1,460-byte TCP payload on a standard 1,500-byte Ethernet MTU
receipts.inputs: TCP initial congestion window = 10 segments
receipts.source: RFC 6928 (IETF, Apr 2013); default since Linux 2.6.39 (May 2011)
receipts.falsifier: a path with a smaller MTU, or a server whose congestion window differs from the RFC 6928 default, moves this number — it is the standard case, not a universal constant.

receipts.formula: surface-code patch ≈ 2d², d the code distance
receipts.inputs: this page's stated convention · the exact rotated-code count is 2d²−1
receipts.falsifier: this is the data + ancilla patch alone — routing, magic-state factories and per-patch overhead sit on top of it, and for real computation can rival or exceed the patch itself.

receipts.formula: d = 2⌈t / −log₁₀r⌉ − 1 · patch = 2d² · logical = ⌊N / patch⌋
receipts.inputs: r = p/p_th = 1/2 · N = 10⁵ · target p_L = 10⁻⁹ → d = 59, patch 6,962
receipts.falsifier: assumes A = 1 in p_L ≈ A(p/p_th)^⌊(d+1)/2⌋; a real device's prefactor moves the required distance, and the bare-patch caveat above applies on top.

receipts.formula: d = 2⌈t / −log₁₀r⌉ − 1 · patch = 2d² · logical = ⌊N / patch⌋
receipts.inputs: r = p/p_th = 1/20 · N = 10⁴ · target p_L = 10⁻⁹ → d = 13, patch 338
receipts.falsifier: B wins on this model, not on any measured device — no machine has yet fielded anything close to 29 below-threshold logical qubits, and The Race's own table is the count that matters.

receipts.inputs: d = 59 vs d = 13 at the ≈2d² convention · the exact 2d²−1 counts give 20.65, a 0.3% difference
receipts.falsifier: compares two patches at one shared 10⁻⁹ target; move the target and both distances move, so the factor is not a constant property of the two machines.

receipts.formula: largest physical-qubit milestone of 2023 ÷ largest of 2019
receipts.inputs: 1,180 (Atom Computing, 2023-10) ÷ 53 (Google Sycamore, 2019-10) = 22.3×
receipts.falsifier: a hand-curated milestone set, not a census — it tracks the largest chip anyone announced, so one unlisted machine moves it. “Physical qubits” also spans fabricated sites, controlled qubits and qubits good enough to compute with; the 1,180 are trap sites.

receipts.value: under a tenth the qubits of 2023's largest chip
receipts.formula: Willow's physical count ÷ each 2023 chip above 1,000 qubits
receipts.falsifier: this sentence previously read “smaller than its own 2019 chip,” which was false — Willow (105) is about twice Sycamore (53). See correction 1. The surviving claim is only about 2023's largest chips.

receipts.formula: 2d²−1 physical qubits for a rotated surface code, plus leakage-removal qubits
receipts.inputs: d = 7 → 2·7²−1 = 97, + 4 leakage-removal = 101, inside Willow's 105
receipts.falsifier: counts one d = 7 patch on one device; it is not a general overhead figure, and the 4 leakage-removal qubits are specific to Willow's implementation.

receipts.formula: fit of log(logical error rate) against distance across a d = 3, 5, 7 series
receipts.inputs: Google Willow processor, per-two-distance-step suppression
receipts.source: Google Quantum AI, Nature 638, 920 (2025); arXiv:2408.13687
receipts.falsifier: the lone d = 5 → 7 step reads closer to 2.1 — 2.14 is the whole-series fit, not any single step, and Λ drifts with calibration.

receipts.formula: |r(t)| = √(x²+y²+z²) must stay ≤ 1 for ρ = (I + r·σ)/2 to be a valid density matrix
receipts.inputs: transverse decay e^(−t/T₂) against longitudinal e^(−t/T₁); with T₂ pushed past 2T₁ the widget's own closed form drives |r| above 1
receipts.falsifier: a Markovian, time-independent-rate bound. Real devices carry slow drift and 1/f noise that no single T₂ captures, and a non-Markovian bath can make an effective T₂ measured over one window meaningless in another.

receipts.value: two-qubit gates (20 ns) before the phase halves
receipts.formula: ⌊ T₂ · ln 2 / t_gate ⌋
receipts.inputs: t_gate = 20 ns · e.g. T₂ = 100 µs → 3,465 gates
receipts.falsifier: counts gate slots inside one coherence half-life, not useful gates — it assumes every gate is perfect and back-to-back, ignores gate error itself, idling, readout and compilation overhead, so a real circuit gets far fewer.

receipts.inputs: the state/unitary/Born/tensor-product postulates this page tabulates
receipts.source: J. von Neumann, Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik (Springer, 1932) — the first fully axiomatic Hilbert-space formulation, incl. the Born-rule and density-matrix machinery
receipts.falsifier: dates the axiomatisation, not the physics: Born's rule is 1926 and Dirac's transformation theory 1927, while decoherence theory and the modern measurement literature are decades later. The claim is only that quantum computing adds no new postulate.

receipts.inputs: the standard physical error rate p ≈ 10⁻³ this site uses throughout (qec.html's threshold widget, logical-qubit.html's calculator, bitcoin.html's estimator)
receipts.source: the resource-estimation convention, not a device datasheet: Webber et al., AVS Quantum Science 4, 013801 (2022) and Gidney et al., arXiv:2603.28846 both cost surface-code machines at p ≈ 10⁻³, and the best reported two-qubit gate errors sit around that order
receipts.falsifier: this is a modelling assumption rounded to one significant figure, not a measurement of any one machine. Single-qubit gates are one to two orders better, measurement is worse, error varies by platform and drifts with calibration, and quoting it as a device spec would be wrong. It is the number every estimate on this site is built on, which is exactly why it is marked.

receipts.value: about 30% fewer wrong calls than the hand-written rulebooks fast enough to run on a live machine, and about 6% fewer than the slowest and most careful one
receipts.inputs: AlphaQubit vs correlated matching (the real-time-capable baseline) and vs a tensor-network decoder (near-optimal, far too slow to run live)
receipts.source: Bausch et al., “Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors,” Nature 635, 834 (2024), Google DeepMind + Google Quantum AI
receipts.falsifier: the two baselines are not interchangeable, and swapping which one the 30% is measured against is the single most common error in secondary coverage of this result. The real-device data is d = 3 and d = 5; the d = 11 result is simulation only. AlphaQubit is also still too slow to decode in real time, so this is accuracy, not a shipped capability.

receipts.formula: Λⁿ suppression after n steps of d → d+2 · n = ⌊log 1000 / log Λ⌋
receipts.inputs: Λ = 2.14 (Willow, regressed across d = 3, 5, 7) · log 1000 / log 2.14 = 9.08 → 9 whole steps
receipts.falsifier: Λ is one device's measured suppression at one calibration, and this extrapolates it nine steps past where it was measured (d = 7 → 23). Nothing guarantees Λ holds constant that far out; new error mechanisms appear at scale.

receipts.formula: 2d² − 1 for a rotated surface-code patch
receipts.inputs: nine Λ-steps from d = 5 → d = 23 · 2·23²−1 = 1,057
receipts.falsifier: this buys ≈ 1,000× of the 1,000,000× the 10⁻⁹ target actually needs — the page says so in the same sentence. The full million takes 19 steps to d = 43 and 3,697 qubits, and even that excludes routing and magic-state factories. qec.html reaches the same 1,057 by a different route (p/p_th = 1/10 to 10⁻¹²); the agreement is a coincidence of both landing on d = 23, not a confirmation.

receipts.value: 99.5% two-qubit and 99.8% single-qubit gate fidelity, with the two-qubit gate itself running in 100 nanoseconds
receipts.inputs: silicon spin qubits, January 2022 — one of three groups (RIKEN/QuTech, TU Delft, UNSW) that cleared the fault-tolerance threshold simultaneously
receipts.source: Noiri, Takeda, Nakajima, Kobayashi, Sammak, Scappucci et al., Nature 601, 338–342 (2022)
receipts.falsifier: a gate fidelity above threshold in a two-qubit device says nothing about whether it survives at scale — the page says so in the next paragraph. Three simultaneous results also means the threshold-crossing is the field's, not one group's.

receipts.value: single- and two-qubit control fidelities above 99% across all four devices tested, with state-preparation-and-measurement fidelity up to 99.9%
receipts.inputs: silicon spin-qubit unit cells fabricated in a 300 mm semiconductor foundry (imec), not a university cleanroom — which is the thesis being tested
receipts.source: Steinacker, Dumoulin Stuyck, Lim, Tanttu, Feng et al. (Diraq/UNSW), “Industry-compatible silicon spin-qubit unit cells exceeding 99% fidelity,” Nature 646, 81–87 (2025)
receipts.falsifier: “unit cells” means a handful of qubits, not hundreds wired together — none of this is at the qubit counts the four leading modalities have reached, and whether control wiring and crosstalk stay manageable as the count climbs is untested.

receipts.value: “represent evidence for the presence of Majorana zero modes in the reported devices”
receipts.inputs: what Nature's editorial team said the Majorana 1 paper did NOT do, published alongside it
receipts.source: editorial note accompanying Microsoft Azure Quantum et al., “Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices,” Nature 638, 651 (2025)
receipts.falsifier: this is an editorial caveat on one paper, not a verdict on topological qubits. Microsoft disputes the reading, named physicists are split on the record in both directions, and the underlying question is unresolved rather than settled against them — which is the point the paragraph makes.

receipts.formula: min Σ c_ij x_ij subject to every supply used and every demand met
receipts.inputs: 2 sources × 3 destinations, 6 routes · ships 15 S1→D1, 15 S1→D3, 20 S2→D2
receipts.falsifier: the optimum of this one toy instance, found by exhaustive integer search AND by the LP relaxation (which agrees because the constraint matrix is totally unimodular — 461 square submatrices checked). Change a single cost and the plan changes; nothing here generalises to a real network.

receipts.inputs: northwest-corner plan 300 · true optimum 240
receipts.falsifier: 25% is this instance's gap, not a property of the northwest-corner rule — the rule is a way to get a feasible starting point fast, and its overspend on another instance could be anything.

receipts.value: For k = 6 that is 2.45, and 3 sits comfortably under 2.45 × 2
receipts.formula: greedy ≤ H(k) · OPT, H(k) = 1 + 1/2 + … + 1/k
receipts.inputs: H(6) = 2.45 · greedy takes 3 sets · optimum is 2 · bound = 4.9
receipts.falsifier: a worst-case guarantee, not a typical one — greedy is usually far closer than H(k), and the bound is only tight on adversarial instances. It also depends on k being the largest set size, not the number of sets.

receipts.formula: EVPI = E[profit | perfect forecast] − E[profit at the stochastic optimum]
receipts.inputs: newsvendor, cost 2 / price 5, demand 20 or 60 at probability ½ · Q* = 60 earns 80 · perfect information earns 120
receipts.falsifier: EVPI prices a forecast that is exactly right every time, which nobody sells. It is an upper bound on what any real forecast can be worth, not a budget.

receipts.formula: VSS = E[profit at the stochastic optimum] − E[profit at the plug-in-the-mean plan]
receipts.inputs: Q* = 60 earns 80 · ordering the mean demand (40) earns 70
receipts.falsifier: VSS is non-negative by construction, so a positive value proves nothing on its own — what matters is whether it is large enough to justify the modelling effort, and on this instance it is one sixth of the perfect-information value.

receipts.value: 12,000 random |ψ⟩ (unique complex α,β on the Bloch sphere), all four measurement outcomes each, corrected state matches the original to within 10⁻¹⁵ up to global phase
receipts.formula: exact state-vector simulation of the teleportation circuit + the four Pauli correction maps
receipts.inputs: 12,000 trials · measured max phase-fixed difference 8.4×10⁻¹⁶
receipts.falsifier: noiseless, exact linear algebra — it proves the protocol's algebra, not that any device can run it. The 10⁻¹⁵ is floating-point round-off, not an error budget.

receipts.value: 500 random bipartite states reconstruct exactly from their SVD (error < 10⁻¹⁴)
receipts.formula: Schmidt decomposition via SVD; reduced-density-matrix eigenvalues compared against λᵢ²
receipts.inputs: 500 random states across dimensions 2×2 … 3×4 · measured max error 4.8×10⁻¹⁵
receipts.falsifier: random states are generically full-Schmidt-rank, so this exercises the typical case, not the degenerate ones (product states, maximally entangled) where numerical rank decisions are delicate. Those two are checked separately by name.

receipts.formula: quantum phase estimation → continued-fraction recovery of the period r
receipts.inputs: 1,189 trials with s coprime to r (recovers r exactly, 100%) · 811 with s not coprime (recovers r/gcd(s,r), a genuine divisor, 100%)
receipts.falsifier: the non-coprime cases do NOT recover r — they recover a divisor of it, which is why Shor's algorithm retries. A 100% figure here is about the continued-fraction step behaving as specified, not about factoring succeeding on one shot.

receipts.formula: dθᵢ/dt = −K Σⱼ Jᵢⱼ sin(θᵢ − θⱼ), Euler, dt = 0.04 — the coupling half of Wang & Roychowdhury's rule, injection locking omitted
receipts.inputs: 300 random starts · each run 100,000 further steps · max residual phase change 3.5×10⁻¹⁷
receipts.falsifier: these states are stationary, not “stuck at a bad arrangement” — the closest any comes to a clean 0/π read is about 1.1 rad, and the widget's absolute read-off still reaches the optimum about 70% of the time. The shortfall is the unpinned global phase, not a worse spin configuration.

receipts.value: every discrete local minimum on this graph is a global optimum — four assignments, two arrangements and their mirror images
receipts.formula: exhaustive enumeration of all 2⁵ = 32 spin assignments, then a single-spin-flip local-minimum test on each
receipts.inputs: 5-cycle with J = −1 plus chords (0,2) and (1,3) with J = +1 · best energy −5 · 6 of 7 edges satisfied
receipts.falsifier: true of this 5-node graph only, and “local minimum” here means discrete single-spin-flip — the continuous phase dynamics have their own fixed points, which is the whole point of the sentence around it. The page said “only one” until 2026-09-04 (correction 3).

receipts.value: a 2,000-node machine and, separately, a fully-connected 100-spin machine
receipts.inputs: the two coherent-Ising-machine demonstrations published the same week of 2016 — the two ends of the connectivity-versus-count trade-off
receipts.source: Inagaki et al., Science 354, 603 (2016) (2,000 time-multiplexed pulses, measurement-and-feedback coupling); McMahon et al., Science 354, 614 (2016) (100 spins, every pair optically coupled)
receipts.falsifier: node count and connectivity are not comparable currencies — 2,000 weakly-coupled nodes and 100 all-to-all ones solve different problem shapes, and neither number is a claim about beating a classical solver.

receipts.value: E_C is held at an illustrative, representative 250 MHz throughout; real designs typically sit within a factor of two of that
receipts.inputs: the charging energy the widget fixes while the E_J/E_C slider moves
receipts.source: Koch, Yu, Gambetta, Houck, Schuster, Majer, Blais, Devoret, Girvin & Schoelkopf, arXiv cond-mat/0703002 (Phys. Rev. A 76, 042319 (2007)) — the transmon paper whose E_J/E_C ≫ 1 regime the slider stays inside
receipts.falsifier: a fixed illustrative value, not a device spec — real E_C is a design choice, and the widget's spectrum would shift with it. The point the widget makes is the shape of the anharmonicity-versus-charge-noise trade-off, which does not depend on the exact value.

receipts.value: roughly an order-of-magnitude error reduction relative to the state of the art at realistic transmon parameters
receipts.inputs: DRAG pulse shaping against the prior state of the art, at realistic transmon parameters
receipts.source: Motzoi, Gambetta, Rebentrost & Wilhelm, arXiv 0901.0534 (Phys. Rev. Lett. 103, 110501 (2009))
receipts.falsifier: the comparison baseline is the paper's own state of the art in 2009, not any modern gate — an earlier version of this page misattributed that baseline, which is why the comparison is spelled out here rather than left as a bare 10×.

receipts.value: a classical recommendation-system algorithm polylogarithmic in dimension under ℓ²-norm sample-and-query access
receipts.inputs: the result that collapsed the flagship quantum recommendation-system speedup (Kerenidis & Prakash) to no exponential separation
receipts.source: Ewin Tang, “A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems,” arXiv:1807.04271 (2018)
receipts.falsifier: the ℓ²-norm sample-and-query access model is an ASSUMPTION about how the classical algorithm reaches its data, chosen to mirror what QRAM would give the quantum one. Change that assumption and the comparison changes; “dequantized” means “under comparable data-access assumptions,” not “on a laptop with a CSV.”

receipts.value: Var[∂θC] decays exponentially in qubit count n
receipts.inputs: random parameterised circuits deep enough to form approximate 2-designs
receipts.source: McClean, Boixo, Smelyanskiy, Babbush & Neven, “Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes,” arXiv:1803.11173 (Nature Communications 9, 4812 (2018))
receipts.falsifier: conditional on the ansatz forming an approximate 2-design — shallow, structured or problem-informed ansatze can avoid the plateau, and a great deal of VQE work exists precisely to do that. This is a statement about random circuits, not a proof that variational methods cannot work.

receipts.value: a proven exponential advantage for learning from quantum experiments
receipts.inputs: a quantum machine learning coherently from quantum experiments, versus any classical learner given the same experimental access
receipts.source: Huang, Broughton, Cotler, Chen, Li, Mohseni, Neven, Babbush, Kueng, Preskill & McClean, “Quantum advantage in learning from experiments,” arXiv:2112.00778 (Science 376, 1182 (2022))
receipts.falsifier: the advantage is for learning about QUANTUM data with coherent quantum memory — it says nothing about quantum ML on classical datasets, which is the claim most “quantum AI” coverage is actually making, and which the same group's arXiv:2011.01938 argues against.
